title: Lecture 1: Algorithmic Thinking, Peak Finding
notes: A 1D peak finding problem: an element a[i] is a peak iff a[i] >= a[i-1] and a[i] >= a[i+1].
Straightforward linear scan takes Theta(n) time.
Divide-and-conquer binary search achieves Theta(log n) time.
2D peak finding: an element is a peak if >= all 4 neighbors. Divide-and-conquer achieves O(n log m) time.

transcript.text: Welcome to 6.006, Introduction to Algorithms. I am Srini Devadas.
This course focuses on efficient algorithms for real-world computational problems.
Let us define 1D peak finding. In an array of numbers, position i is a peak if it is greater than or equal to both its neighbors.
If we look at middle element a[n/2] and it is less than a[n/2-1], there must be a peak on the left half.
Writing the recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + Theta(1), yielding Theta(log n).

title: Lecture 2: Models of Computation, Document Distance
notes: Random Access Machine (RAM) model: constant time memory access in word-sized operations.
Python cost model: list operations, dictionary hashing, and pointer manipulations.
Document distance: computing cosine similarity between term frequency vectors.

transcript.text: Today we address how we measure computational efficiency: models of computation.
In the RAM model, instructions execute one by one and memory words can be accessed in O(1) time.
Document distance measures similarity between two text files using inner product of word frequency vectors.
Dividing the dot product by vector lengths yields cosine of angle theta.

title: Lecture 3: Insertion Sort, Merge Sort
notes: Insertion Sort: incremental in-place sorting taking Theta(n^2) worst-case time, Theta(n) best-case.
Merge Sort: divide into halves, sort recursively, and merge two sorted lists in Theta(n) time.
Recurrence relation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) solves to Theta(n log n).

transcript.text: Welcome back. Today we delve into sorting, one of the most fundamental problems in CS.
Insertion sort keeps a prefix sorted and inserts the next element by shifting larger elements right.
Merge sort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts, and merges in linear time.
Using recursion trees to analyze T(n) = 2T(n/2) + c*n reveals log n levels each costing c*n.

title: Lecture 4: Heaps and Heap Sort
notes: A binary heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the max-heap property: A[parent(i)] >= A[i].
Max-Heapify runs in O(log n) time.
Build-Max-Heap converts an unordered array into a heap in O(n) linear time.
Heapsort achieves O(n log n) sorting in-place.

transcript.text: In Lecture 4, we examine heaps: a tree-based data structure represented cleanly inside an array.
For node at index i, left child is 2i, right child is 2i+1, parent is floor(i/2).
Max-heapify corrects a violation at the root by floating the larger child upward.
Surprising theorem: Build-Heap runs in linear O(n) time because most nodes sit near the leaves.

title: Lecture 5: Binary Search Trees, BST Sort
notes: BST invariant: for any node x, keys in left subtree <= x.key <= keys in right subtree.
Operations insert, find, delete, predecessor, successor run in O(h) time where h is tree height.
In degenerate cases, h can be O(n). Balanced trees guarantee h = O(log n).

transcript.text: Lecture 5 introduces Binary Search Trees (BSTs) for fast dynamic searching and ranking.
The fundamental BST invariant allows binary search logic on non-contiguous dynamic nodes.
In-order tree traversal visits keys in strictly sorted order in O(n) time.

title: Lecture 6: AVL Trees, AVL Sort
notes: AVL balance property: heights of left and right children differ by at most 1.
An AVL tree with n nodes has height h < 1.44 log_2(n).
Single and double tree rotations restore balance in O(1) time after insertions and deletions.

transcript.text: Today Prof. Erik Demaine shows us AVL trees, the first self-balancing binary search trees invented.
We define balance factor as height(left) minus height(right). In AVL trees, this must be in {-1, 0, 1}.
Rotations rearrange pointers locally in O(1) time while strictly maintaining the BST search invariant.

title: Lecture 7: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, Lower Bounds
concept_name: Linear Time Sorting & Comparison Lower Bounds
notes: Decision tree model proves any comparison-based sort requires Omega(n log n) comparisons.
Counting sort operates in O(n + k) time for integers bounded in [0, k].
Radix sort sorts numbers digit-by-digit stably from least to most significant digit in O(d * (n + b)) time.

transcript.text: Can we sort faster than n log n? We will prove a lower bound for comparison sorts and see linear time sorting.
A decision tree must have at least n! leaves. The height is at least log(n!) = Omega(n log n).
Counting sort escapes this lower bound by using integer array indexing directly.

title: Lecture 8: Hashing with Chaining
notes: Dictionary problem: maintain a set of items under insert, delete, search.
Collision resolution by chaining: linked list in each bucket.
Simple Uniform Hashing assumption: expected chain length is load factor alpha = n/m.
Universal hashing guarantees low collision probability over random choice of hash functions.

transcript.text: Hashing is one of the most widely used techniques in all of computer software.
Map universe U to m buckets using hash function h(k). When two keys collide, chaining stores them in a list.
If table size m is proportional to n, average lookup time is O(1).

title: Lecture 9: Table Doubling, Karp-Rabin
notes: Dynamic table resizing: doubling table size when full yields O(1) amortized cost per insert.
Amortized analysis via banker's / accounting method.
Karp-Rabin string matching algorithm uses rolling hashes to find substrings in O(n + m) expected time.

transcript.text: How do we choose hash table size m when we do not know n in advance? Table doubling and amortized analysis.
When the table fills up, allocate a table of size 2m and re-insert all keys.
Karp-Rabin string matching slides a hash window over text T of length n in linear expected time.

title: Lecture 10: Open Addressing, Cryptographic Hashing
notes: Open addressing stores all keys directly in the table slots without linked lists.
Probing strategies: linear probing, quadratic probing, and double hashing.
Cryptographic hashing properties: collision resistance, preimage resistance, and avalanche effect.

transcript.text: Lecture 10 covers open addressing and cryptographic hash functions like SHA-256.
Linear probing checks h(k)+i mod m, but suffers from primary clustering where clusters grow rapidly.
Double hashing uses two independent hash functions to achieve uniform permutation probing.

title: Lecture 11: Integer Arithmetic, Karatsuba Multiplication
notes: Grade school multiplication takes Theta(d^2) time for d-digit integers.
Karatsuba's trick reduces 4 recursive subproblems to 3: T(d) = 3T(d/2) + Theta(d).
Achieves O(d^{log_2 3}) approx O(d^{1.585}) time.

transcript.text: Welcome to unit 3 on numerics. Today we look at integer multiplication with arbitrarily many digits.
Grade school algorithm multiplies each digit with every other digit, taking O(n^2) operations.
Karatsuba noticed that (x1*y0 + x0*y1) can be computed using one multiplication and two additions.

title: Lecture 12: Square Roots, Newton's Method
notes: Finding square root of a via finding zeros of f(x) = x^2 - a.
Newton's iteration formula: x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k).
Quadratic convergence: number of accurate digits doubles with each iteration.

transcript.text: How do computer chips calculate square roots and division to high precision? Newton's method.
We draw a tangent line at (x_k, f(x_k)) and find where it intercepts the x-axis.
The error squares at every step: 10 digits becomes 20 digits, then 40 digits, then 80 digits.

title: Lecture 13: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
notes: Graph representations: adjacency lists vs adjacency matrices.
BFS explores vertices in order of increasing distance from start vertex s.
Maintains queue frontier; visits each vertex and edge once in O(V + E) time.
Computes shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

transcript.text: Today we begin graph algorithms with Breadth-First Search, or BFS.
A graph G = (V, E) can be directed or undirected. We represent it with adjacency lists for efficiency.
BFS discovers all vertices at distance 1, then distance 2, then distance k, using a FIFO queue.

title: Lecture 14: Depth-First Search (DFS), Topological Sort
notes: DFS explores graph deeply along paths before backtracking.
Classification of edges: tree edges, back edges, forward edges, cross edges.
A directed graph is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) iff DFS produces no back edges.
Topological sorting: reverse order of finishing times in DAG runs in O(V + E) time.

transcript.text: Depth-First Search (DFS) recursively traverses paths to their ends before backtracking.
Every edge gets classified during search. A back edge points to an active ancestor, revealing a cycle.
Topological sort orders tasks respecting dependencies: sort vertices by reverse finishing times.

title: Lecture 15: Single-Source Shortest Paths Problem
notes: Shortest path weight delta(s, v): minimum weight over all paths from s to v.
Negative-weight edges and negative-weight cycles.
Generic relaxation framework: if d[v] > d[u] + w(u, v), then d[v] = d[u] + w(u, v).
Optimal substructure property: subpaths of shortest paths are also shortest paths.

transcript.text: Unit 4 is Shortest Paths. Today we set up the general framework and edge relaxation.
Edge weights represent distances, transit times, or financial costs.
Edge relaxation gradually tightens upper bounds on true distance until all bounds become exact.

title: Lecture 16: Dijkstra's Algorithm
notes: Dijkstra solves single-source shortest paths on graphs with non-negative edge weights.
Greedy strategy: extract minimum distance estimate vertex from priority queue.
With binary min-heap: running time is O((V + E) log V). With Fibonacci heap: O(E + V log V).

transcript.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is the gold standard for routing and navigation systems.
Because all edge weights are non-negative, once a vertex has minimum distance from the frontier, its distance is finalized.
Each vertex is extracted once from the priority queue and each incident edge is relaxed once.

title: Lecture 17: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
notes: Bellman-Ford handles arbitrary edge weights and detects negative-weight cycles.
Relaxes all |E| edges |V| - 1 times in O(V * E) total time.
A final pass checking if any edge can still be relaxed identifies negative cycle reachability.

transcript.text: What happens when edges can have negative weights, such as currency arbitrage? Bellman-Ford.
Any simple path contains at most |V|-1 edges. So relaxing all edges |V|-1 times suffices to find all shortest paths.
If an edge can still be relaxed on pass |V|, that edge is part of or reachable from a negative weight cycle.

title: Lecture 18: Speeding up Dijkstra & Heuristic Search
notes: Bidirectional Dijkstra search explores simultaneously from start and destination, cutting search space.
Goal-directed search (A*): modifies edge weights using potential function h(u).
Consistent (monotone) heuristics guarantee optimal shortest paths without reopening nodes.

transcript.text: In practice, Dijkstra explores a full circular wave of vertices. Today we show how to aim the search at the target.
Bidirectional search runs Dijkstra forward from s and backwards from t until the two search frontiers collide.
A* search introduces a heuristic estimate h(v) of remaining distance to t, steering exploration straight toward the goal.

title: Lecture 19: Dynamic Programming I: Fibonacci, Shortest Paths
notes: Dynamic Programming: memoization and subproblem reuse.
Fibonacci naive recursion O(2^n) drops to O(n) with memoized table.
The 5-step DP recipe: define subproblems, guess choices, relate subproblem solutions, recurse & memoize, solve original problem.

transcript.text: Welcome to Dynamic Programming! DP is arguably the most powerful general algorithm design technique.
Naive recursive Fibonacci computes identical subtrees repeatedly, causing an exponential explosion.
Memoization caches return values in a table. Once computed, subproblems take O(1) lookup time.

title: Lecture 20: Dynamic Programming II: Text Justification, Blackjack
notes: Text justification: break words into lines minimizing total line raggedness penalty (cube of blank spaces).
Subproblems on suffixes words[i:]: guess line break position j > i.
Blackjack: perfect play against dealer with known card deck.

transcript.text: Today we apply Dynamic Programming to text justification (like LaTeX line breaking) and Blackjack.
Define DP[i] as optimal raggedness for suffix of words from index i to end.
Guess where the current line ends at j. Running time is O(n^2) where n is word count.

title: Lecture 21: Dynamic Programming III: Parenthesization, Edit Distance, Knapsack
notes: Edit Distance: minimum cost to transform string X into Y using insert, delete, replace.
Subproblems on prefixes: DP[i, j] matches X[i] and Y[j].
0-1 Knapsack: maximize value subject to weight constraint W, solved in pseudo-polynomial O(n*W) time.

transcript.text: Edit distance and knapsack are two quintessential 2-dimensional Dynamic Programming problems.
In edit distance, we either insert, delete, or replace characters at indices i and j.
In 0-1 Knapsack, item i is either taken or not taken, consuming capacity w_i.

title: Lecture 22: Dynamic Programming IV: Guitar Fingering, Tetris, Super Mario
notes: Guitar fingering: mapping musical notes to hand finger positions minimizing physical transition difficulty.
Tetris and Super Mario Bros: modeling video game stages as state reachability graphs under DP transitions.
Complexity of playing video games: why Nintendo games are NP-hard.

transcript.text: In DP IV, Prof. Erik Demaine shows fun applications: guitar fingering and video game algorithms.
For guitar fingering, state is (note_index, finger_position) with transition costs measuring biomechanical strain.
We model games as DAGs of reachable states to find the globally optimal play sequence.

title: Lecture 23: Computational Complexity
notes: Class P: problems solvable in polynomial time O(n^k).
Class NP: problems whose candidate solutions can be verified in polynomial time.
NP-completeness and polynomial-time reductions: showing problem A is as hard as problem B.
Cook-Levin Theorem: Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete.

transcript.text: Today we ask the million-dollar Millennium Prize problem: Does P equal NP?
P is the set of decision problems solvable in polynomial time on a deterministic machine.
If any NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time, then every problem in NP can be solved in polynomial time.

title: Lecture 24: Topics in Algorithms Research
notes: Modern research frontiers: streaming algorithms, sublinear time algorithms, and quantum algorithms.
Cache-oblivious data structures and geometric folding algorithms.
Summary of 6.006 core themes: design paradigms, analysis techniques, and practical impact.

transcript.text: Welcome to the final lecture of 6.006. Today we discuss current frontiers in algorithms research.
We recap the major paradigms: Divide & Conquer, Greedy, Dynamic Programming, and Graph Traversals.
Thank you all for an exceptional semester of algorithmic problem solving!
